Mont Blanc is the highest peak in the Alps at fifteen thousand seven hundred seventy-four feet, straddling the border of France, Italy, and Switzerland in the Western Alps. Its proximity to European population centers, moderate altitude, and relative accessibility make it the most popular high-altitude destination in Europe. Tens of thousands summit annually, yet the mountain claims dozens of lives each year. The peak is accessible via multiple routes from the Chamonix valley in France. The standard route is non-technical but requires acclimatization and glacier travel. The Goûter Route is the most popular path, funneling thousands of climbers up a single corridor where rockfall and altitude sickness exact a steady toll. Michel Paccard and Jacques Balmat made the first recorded ascent in seventeen eighty-six, spurring the birth of modern mountaineering and Alpine tourism. Perpetual snow and extensive glaciers define the peak, but glacier retreat has made routes progressively more rockfall-prone and hazardous. Summer conditions in July and August draw the vast majority of climbers, while winter ascents are rare and extremely dangerous. All three nations dispute boundary claims on the peak itself, though France claims Mont Blanc as its highest point.
